Should you drink apple cider vinegar before breakfast? In this video, I explain how organic apple cider vinegar (ACV) may help reduce post-meal blood sugar spikes, why choosing organic ACV matters, and the safest way to drink it. You'll also learn the recommended amount, why it should always be diluted, and how using a straw may help protect your tooth enamel. While apple cider vinegar may support blood sugar management for some people, it should complement—not replace—a healthy lifestyle and any treatment recommended by your healthcare professional. Research suggests ACV may have modest benefits for fasting and post-meal blood sugar, but it is not a cure for diabetes.

text:
Should you take a daily aspirin after 60? The answer depends on why you are taking it. Aspirin can help some people who already have cardiovascular disease, but taking it routinely to prevent a first heart attack or stroke may cause more harm than benefit in many older adults.

In this video, Dr. Rehan explains the difference between primary prevention and secondary prevention and why that distinction matters for seniors taking aspirin every day.

You’ll learn:

Whether adults over 60 should take daily aspirin
What primary prevention means
What secondary prevention means
Why aspirin can increase bleeding risk
When aspirin may still be recommended after a heart attack or stroke
Why a prior stent or bypass can change the decision
Why older adults should not start or stop daily aspirin without speaking to their healthcare professional

Current American Heart Association guidance says healthy adults without known cardiovascular disease generally should not take daily low-dose aspirin unless advised by their healthcare professional. For people over 70, routine aspirin use to prevent a first heart attack or stroke can do more harm than good because bleeding risk increases with age.

Aspirin still has an important role in secondary prevention. People who have already had a heart attack, stroke, coronary stent, or bypass surgery may be advised to continue aspirin as part of their treatment plan.

Because aspirin reduces clot formation, it can also increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and hemorrhagic stroke. The balance between cardiovascular benefit and bleeding risk should be individualized.

If you currently take aspirin every day, do not stop it on your own. Ask your doctor why you are taking it and whether it is still appropriate for your current health history.

Coffee after 50: is it good or bad for your heart? Coffee and caffeine can temporarily raise blood pressure and heart rate in some people, but that does not necessarily mean you need to stop drinking coffee.

In this video, Dr. Rehan explains what coffee really does to your cardiovascular system and the three things adults over 50 should pay attention to: blood pressure, heart-rate response, and total caffeine intake.

You'll learn:

Does coffee raise blood pressure?
Why caffeine can temporarily increase blood pressure
Whether coffee causes hypertension
Why some people experience heart palpitations or a racing heartbeat after coffee
How caffeine sensitivity differs from person to person
How much caffeine is considered safe for most adults
Why cup size matters when counting your daily coffee intake
How coffee compares with high-caffeine energy drinks
When symptoms after caffeine should be discussed with a healthcare professional

The latest 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement reports that for most adults, consuming up to about 400 mg of caffeine per day—roughly 3 to 5 eight-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee—is generally considered safe. Individual responses vary based on factors including genetics, metabolism, age, habitual caffeine intake and medical conditions.

Caffeine can cause temporary increases in blood pressure, heart rate and alertness, and some people may experience palpitations, anxiety or sleep disruption. However, moderate caffeinated coffee consumption has also been associated with lower risks of some cardiovascular conditions in observational research. These associations do not prove that coffee itself prevents heart disease.

If you have high blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, significant palpitations, medication concerns or strong caffeine sensitivity, discuss your individual caffeine intake with your healthcare professional.

stabilizes. But the moment you stand up quickly,
gravity suddenly pulls the blood downward towards 
your legs. Your heart must immediately pump in
order to push the blood back to the brain. Young 
bodies adjust quickly. But as we age, some people
experiences dizziness, lightadedness, blurred 
vision, feeling unstable for a few seconds. This
reaction is known as orthostatic hypotension or 
orthostatic or positional blood pressure drop. In
some cases, it can increase the risk of falls. In 
the older adults, your body is designed to adapt
to movement, but certain changes in pressures 
in postures can overwhelm the circular system.
Therefore, giving your body just a few seconds 
to adjust can make a lot of difference. So,
here's a simple fix. Here's what cardiologists 
often recommend. When you wake up in the morning,
sit on the edge of the bed for about 30 seconds. 
Then take small few rapid deep breaths and then
stand up gradually. This allows your heart and 
blood vessels to adjust smoothly instead of
suddenly. A small pause can reduce dizziness and 
improve circulation. While we are talking about
mornings, there are two other habits that support 
cardiovascular health. First, always drink a
glass of water after waking up. During sleep, the 
body loses fluid through breathing and sweating,
which is known as insensible fluid loss. Second, 
move your body gently. A short stretch or slow
walk activates circulation and prepares the 
cardiovascular system for the day. Even 5 minutes
of light movement can also help. Heart disease 
rarely happens overnight. Instead, it develops
slowly through years of habits. That's why small 
improvements in daily outcomes can have a powerful
effect over time. Protecting your heart doesn't 
always require major lifestyle changes. Sometimes
it begins with simple awareness. And speaking 
of daily habits, did you know that the way you
walk may actually reveal hidden heart problems? 
Cardiologists sometimes detect cardiovascular risk
simply by observing patients walking speed. In the 
next video, I'll explain how your walking pattern
can reveal important clues about your heart 
health. If you want to learn more about protecting

Can instant oatmeal spike your blood sugar? Oatmeal can be a heart-healthy whole grain, but the type of oats you choose—and what you add to them—can make a difference for blood glucose, especially if you have type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance.

Instant oats are processed into thinner pieces and generally digest faster than steel-cut or less-processed oats. Some flavored instant oatmeal products also contain added sugars, which can further increase the carbohydrate load of your breakfast.

In this video, Dr. Rehan explains why:

Instant oatmeal may raise blood sugar faster than less-processed oats
Steel-cut and minimally processed oats can have a lower glycemic impact
Added sugar in flavored oatmeal matters
Portion size and total carbohydrate intake affect blood glucose
Pairing carbohydrates with protein, fiber, or healthy fats—such as nuts or eggs—may help create a more balanced meal
People with diabetes should pay attention to their own post-meal glucose response

Oats also contain beta-glucan soluble fiber and can be part of a healthy eating pattern. The goal is not necessarily to eliminate oatmeal, but to choose the right type, watch added sugars and portions, and build a balanced breakfast.

Blood sugar responses vary from person to person. Speak with your healthcare professional or diabetes care team about the eating pattern and glucose targets that are appropriate for you.

Heart attack symptoms are not always dramatic. Some people may experience shortness of breath, weakness, nausea, dizziness, sweating or unusual fatigue in addition to—or sometimes instead of—obvious chest pain.

Is 12 chair stands in 30 seconds a good score after 60? The answer depends on your age and sex—there is no single passing score that applies to every older adult.

The 30-Second Chair Stand Test is a simple functional test used to assess lower-body strength and endurance. You stand up fully from a chair, sit back down, and repeat as many times as possible for 30 seconds without using your hands.

In this Short, Dr. Rehan explains:

Whether 12 chair stands is a “good” score
Why there is no universal passing number
Why chair-stand scores change with age
Why men and women may have different reference ranges
What the 30-second chair stand test measures
Why a low score does not automatically mean you are frail or sick
How the full chair-stand test can help assess senior fitness, mobility, and lower-body strength

Common reference ranges vary considerably by age and sex. For example, widely used Senior Fitness Test reference data show approximate ranges of 14–19 repetitions for men and 12–17 for women ages 60–64, while expected scores are lower in older age groups.

That means 12 repetitions could fall within the expected range for one older adult but below the reference range for another.

A low chair-stand score is not a diagnosis by itself. Clinicians interpret the test alongside factors such as age, mobility, balance, medical history and other fall-risk information. The test is one component of functional assessment in older adults.

Watch the related full video to see how to perform the 30-second chair stand test correctly, compare your score with age- and sex-based reference ranges, and understand what your result may mean.

Checking your blood pressure at home? Drinking coffee right before your BP reading can temporarily raise your blood pressure and may make the measurement less representative of your normal resting level.

For a more accurate home blood pressure reading, the American Heart Association recommends avoiding caffeine, smoking and exercise for at least 30 minutes before checking your blood pressure. You should also sit quietly for about five minutes before taking the measurement.

In this short video, Dr. Rehan explains:

Why caffeine can temporarily raise blood pressure
Why you should wait before checking BP after coffee
How to prepare for an accurate home blood pressure reading
Why one temporary rise does not automatically mean you have hypertension
Why proper blood pressure monitoring becomes especially important after 50 and 60

Caffeine can temporarily increase blood pressure and heart rate because it increases sympathetic nervous-system activity. Individual responses vary depending on age, habitual caffeine use, metabolism and medical conditions.

A single blood pressure reading is not enough to diagnose hypertension. Home blood pressure readings should be taken correctly and interpreted over time with your healthcare professional.

you've even had your breakfast. You didn't eat
dessert. You didn't sneak at a midnight snack. 
In fact, you haven't eaten anything for nearly
10 hours. So, where did that sugar come from? 
Most people immediately blame the last night's
dinner. But what if dinner isn't the real reason? 
What if your body has been quietly raising your
blood sugars while you were asleep without you

seven reasons why this can happen which one are

unknowingly make every single evening. If you

interventional cardiologist and dermatologist. One
of the questions I hear most often from patients 
is doc I didn't eat anything so why is my morning
sugar higher than yesterday? The answer is really 
as simple as people expected. Let's start with
the explanation that surprises almost everyone. 
Factor number one, the body's morning alarm clock.
Imagine your body has its own alarm clock. Around 
3:00 or 4 in the morning, long before you open
your eyes, it begins preparing for the day ahead. 
Your brain needs fuel for that. Your muscles need
energy. So, your liver quietly releases some of it 
stored sugar into your bloodstream by the process
known as glycogenolysis. It's completely normal 
process. Doctors call it the dawn phenomenon. Now,
here's where things become interesting and a 
bit complicated. If your body responds well
to insulin, that extra sugar is usually handled 
without much change in your blood glucose levels.
But if insulin isn't working as efficiently as can 
happen with insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes,
that same normal process may leave you waking up 
with a higher blood sugar reading. Which means
that number on your meter doesn't automatically 
mean you failed yesterday. Sometimes it's simply
how your body responded overnight. But 
if your liver isn't the only explanation,
what else could it be? Factor number two, the 
dinner you already forgot. Many people focus on
breakfast. Doctors often spend just as much time 
asking about dinner. Not because carbohydrates
are bad. They're not. The question is, how much? 
What kind? And when? Think about the two different
evenings. One person finishes a balanced dinner 
at 6:30 p.m. Another eats a large plate of refined
carbohydrates while watching television at 10 p.m. 
By morning, those two bodies may not be in the
same place. As we get older, digestion, activity 
levels, and insulin sensitivity can all change.
A meal your body handled easily 20 years ago 
may affect your overnight blood sugars very
differently today. That's why many healthcare 
providers encourage looking for patterns rather
than judging one meal. Some people even keep a 
simple notebook of dinner time, what they ate, and
their fasting glucose the next morning. Over time, 
those patterns often become much more informative
than any single reading. But food isn't the only 
thing working with while you're asleep. Sometimes
biggest clue has nothing to do with eating 
at all. Fact number three, the missing piece
most people never suspect, sleep. Let me ask you 
something. Have you ever had a week where nothing
about your diet changed, but your morning blood 
sugar suddenly started cliking? For many people,
the answer isn't found in the kitchen. It's found 
in the bedroom. Because while you're asleep, your
body isn't simply turned off. Your brain is still 
working. Your heart is pumping. Your hormones are
still working and communicating with every organ 
in your body. Now imagine sleeping only four or
5 hours a day or waking up every hour without 
realizing it or struggling with loud snoring
or pauses in breathing throughout the night. Your 
body doesn't always interpret the that as restful
sleep. Sometimes it interprets it as stress and 
when that happens it may produce more stress
hormones like cortisol, glucagon and adrenaline. 
These hormones are designed to help you survive in
difficult situation but they can also make it 
harder for insulin to do its job effectively.
Think of insulin as the key. On a good night, the 
key turns smoothly. After poor sleep, it's almost
as if the lock becomes stiff. The same key still 
fits. It just does not work as efficiently. That
doesn't mean poor sleep is the only explanation 
for a hard morning reading. But for many people,
it's important piece the puzzle that's easy 
to overlook. So ask yourself, do you wake up
refreshed or do you wake up feeling tired because 
the day has not even begun? If poor sleep has
become your normal, it's worth mentioning to your 
healthcare provider, not just for your energy,
but because sleep quality can influence many 
aspects of overall health, including blood sugar.
But there's another factor that's even easier to 
miss because it happens every single day without
most people thinking about it. Factor number 
four, routine matters more than people realize.
Here's something I've noticed over the years. 
Most people don't intentionally ignore their
treatment plan. Life simply gets busy. Dinner 
is later than usual. Bedtime changes. A dose
gets delayed. The next day starts differently. One 
unusual evening probably won't explain every high
eating. But when small changes become habits, 
they can begin creating patterns. And blood
sugars love pattern. Healthcare providers often 
talk about consistency because the body responds
remarkably well to predictable routines, regular 
meal times, regular sleep, regular activity,
regular medication schedules. All of these pieces 
work together. There's something else many people
don't realize. Some medications prescribed for 
completely different health reasons can also
influence blood sugars. There's a lot of reason to 
stop taking them. Far from it, it's simply another
reason to keep your healthcare team informed 
whenever something changes. One of the most
useful things you can bring to an appointment 
is in perfect glucose number. It's a simple
record. When your readings change, when your 
routine change, when you start new medication,
those detail often tell a much clearer story than 
memory alone. But even then, when medications
stay exactly the same, tiny evening habits can 
quietly push that number higher. Factor five,
the small evening habits that add up. Here's 
something many people find surprising. Sometimes
it's not one big mistake, it's several tiny ones. 
Individually don't they don't seem important,
but together they can create a pattern. Picture 
a typical evening. Dinner is finished. You settle
into your favorite chair. Television is on. 
A handful of crackers, a bowl of cereal,
a flavor yogurt, popcorns, maybe a glass 
of juice because sometimes healthier than
soda. None of those choices automatically 
cause problems. But for someone already
living insulin resistance or diabetes, timing 
and portions may matter more than expected.
Final thoughts. If there is one message I 
hope stayed with you after today's video,
it is this. A high morning blood sugar reading 
doesn't automatically mean you have done something

You may say, “I only drink two cups of coffee a day,” but the size of those cups can completely change how much caffeine you’re actually getting. A small home mug is not the same as a large coffee-shop or office cup.

In this Short, Dr. Rehan explains why adults over 50, 60, and 70 should think about caffeine dose, not just the number of cups they drink.

For most adults, the FDA cites 400 mg of caffeine per day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects, but individual sensitivity varies widely.

So instead of counting only “cups,” pay attention to the actual ounces and caffeine content of what you drink.

Should you stop drinking coffee after 50? For most adults over 50, 60, or 70, age alone is not a reason to give up coffee. What matters more is how caffeine affects your blood pressure, heart rate, symptoms, sleep, and how much you drink.

In this Short, Dr. Rehan explains three things older adults should consider before deciding whether coffee is right for them:

Your blood pressure response to caffeine
Whether coffee causes a racing heart or palpitations
How much coffee and caffeine you drink each day

Caffeine can temporarily increase blood pressure and heart rate in some people, while others tolerate coffee with few noticeable effects. Individual response varies significantly.

According to the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement, up to about 400 mg of caffeine per day—roughly 3 to 5 eight-ounce cups of regular black coffee—is generally considered safe for most adults. However, that is not a target everyone needs to reach, and some people may experience symptoms at much lower amounts.

Adults over 50 do not automatically need to reduce coffee simply because they are getting older. Blood pressure, sleep problems, heart palpitations, medications, underlying heart conditions, and personal caffeine sensitivity may be better reasons to adjust intake.

Is coffee good for your heart—or bad for it? The answer is not simply “good” or “bad.” What matters more is how your body responds to caffeine, how much you drink, and whether coffee affects your blood pressure, heart rate, sleep, or causes palpitations.

In this Short, Dr. Rehan explains why coffee and energy drinks should not be treated as the same thing, especially for adults over 50, 60, and 70.

You’ll learn:

Whether coffee is good or bad for heart health
Why caffeine affects people differently
How coffee can temporarily affect blood pressure and heart rate
Why palpitations, anxiety, or sleep problems may signal caffeine sensitivity
Why total caffeine dose matters
Why energy drinks can be different from ordinary coffee
What older adults should consider before changing their coffee habits

The American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement says that for most adults, up to about 400 mg of caffeine per day, or roughly 3 to 5 eight-ounce cups of regular caffeinated coffee, is generally considered safe. However, individual responses vary significantly.

Moderate caffeinated coffee has also been associated with lower risks of some cardiovascular conditions in observational studies, but these studies do not prove that coffee itself prevents heart disease.

Energy drinks are different. High doses of caffeine from energy drinks and energy shots may raise blood pressure and increase the risk of abnormal heart rhythms, and the AHA specifically warns against simply applying ordinary coffee research to energy drinks.

Does coffee make your heart race, cause palpitations, anxiety, sweating, or disturb your sleep? These symptoms can be signs that you are more sensitive to caffeine and may be getting more than your body comfortably tolerates.

Other symptoms suggesting caffeine sensitivity

Caffeine affects people differently. According to the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement, some people can tolerate moderate coffee intake with few symptoms, while others may experience palpitations, anxiety, or sleep disruption at much lower amounts.

What is Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), and why should you have this cholesterol-related blood test at least once in your lifetime? Lp(a) is a largely inherited cardiovascular risk factor that is not usually measured on a standard cholesterol or lipid panel.
In this video, Dr. Rehan Omer explains why Lp(a) matters even if you already know your LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and total cholesterol.
You’ll learn:
What Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), actually is
Why Lp(a) is different from LDL cholesterol
Why a standard lipid panel may not include Lp(a)
How high Lp(a) can increase heart attack and stroke risk
Why Lp(a) is largely determined by your genes
Who should get an Lp(a) blood test
Why the 2026 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline recommends testing every adult at least once
What an Lp(a) result of 50 mg/dL (125 nmol/L) or higher may mean
Why family history of premature heart disease makes this test especially important
What to do if your Lp(a) is elevated
The 2026 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends measuring Lp(a) at least once in adulthood. An Lp(a) level of 125 nmol/L or 50 mg/dL or higher is considered a cardiovascular risk-enhancing factor and is associated with about a 1.4-fold higher ASCVD risk. Levels around 250 nmol/L or 100 mg/dL are associated with roughly twice the estimated risk. professional.heart.org
Lp(a) is mostly genetically determined and tends to remain relatively stable throughout life. Lifestyle changes usually have little effect on the Lp(a) number itself, which is why repeat testing is generally unnecessary for most people. However, healthy lifestyle choices remain important because your overall heart and stroke risk depends on much more than Lp(a) alone. American College of Cardiology
The American Heart Association estimates that about 1 in 5 people worldwide have elevated Lp(a), often without any symptoms. www.heart.org
If your Lp(a) is high, your healthcare professional may recommend more intensive management of LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, weight, and other cardiovascular risk factors. professional.heart.org

What is “Ozempic vagina” or “Ozempic vulva,” and can semaglutide affect sexual health? In this video, we explain the vulvar, vaginal, body-composition, and sexual-health changes some people report while using Ozempic and other GLP-1 medications.
“Ozempic vagina” is not a medical diagnosis or an established official side effect. The term is commonly used online to describe changes such as loss of fullness around the vulva, looser skin, vaginal dryness, discomfort, or changes in sexual wellbeing noticed during significant weight loss.
In this video, you’ll learn:
* What “Ozempic vagina” and “Ozempic vulva” actually mean
* How rapid or significant weight loss can reduce fat volume around the mons pubis and labia
* Why vaginal dryness may have several causes, including menopause, hormonal changes, hydration, and other health factors
* What current research says about semaglutide and sexual function
* Why GLP-1 weight loss can include some loss of lean body mass
* Why vaginal or sexual symptoms should not automatically be blamed on Ozempic
* When symptoms should be discussed with a healthcare professional
Current evidence does not establish vaginal dryness, vulvar changes, or sexual dysfunction as common direct adverse effects of Ozempic. The official prescribing information lists gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation among its most common adverse reactions.
However, significant weight loss can change fat distribution throughout the body, including the vulvar area. Recent medical discussions of “Ozempic vulva” suggest that volume loss and skin laxity may be related more to substantial weight loss than to a direct toxic effect of semaglutide on vaginal tissue.
Research into GLP-1 medications and sexual function is still developing. A 2026 review found that female-specific evidence remains limited and that the relationship between GLP-1 therapy and sexual function is not yet fully understood.
If you develop persistent vaginal dryness, pain, abnormal bleeding or discharge, urinary symptoms, or sexual difficulties while taking semaglutide, speak with your healthcare professional rather than assuming the medication is the only possible cause.

What do your kidney numbers actually mean? Two important tests—eGFR and uACR—can give very different information about kidney health, especially if you have type 2 diabetes or high blood pressure.

In this video, Dr. Rehan explains why looking at eGFR alone is not enough and why a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, or uACR, can reveal signs of kidney damage even when your eGFR still appears relatively normal.

You'll learn:

What eGFR means on your blood-test report
What the uACR urine test measures
Why diabetes and high blood pressure can damage the kidneys
What protein or albumin in the urine may mean
Why an eGFR below 60 deserves further evaluation
Why a uACR of 30 mg/g or higher may signal kidney damage
Why one abnormal result does not always diagnose chronic kidney disease
How kidney health affects medication dosing and cardiovascular risk
Why heart, kidney, diabetes and metabolic health are closely connected

The 2026 American Diabetes Association Standards of Care recommend checking both eGFR and uACR at least annually in all people with type 2 diabetes. In people who already have chronic kidney disease, testing may be needed more frequently depending on disease stage.

The National Kidney Foundation also emphasizes that both tests are needed for a clearer picture of kidney health: eGFR estimates filtration, while uACR looks for albumin leaking into the urine. A uACR of 30 mg/g or higher can indicate kidney damage even when eGFR is above 60.

The new 2026 cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) guideline also recommends using both eGFR and uACR to characterize chronic kidney disease and guide kidney- and heart-protective treatment.

If you have diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or are over 60, ask your healthcare professional what your eGFR and uACR numbers mean for you.

Over 60? How many times can you stand up from a chair in 30 seconds without using your hands? The 30-Second Chair Stand Test is a simple clinical test used to assess lower-body strength and endurance in older adults.

In this video, Dr. Rehan explains how to perform the 30-second chair stand test, what your score may tell you about leg strength and functional fitness, and why the expected number of chair stands changes with age and sex.

You'll learn:

What the 30-Second Chair Stand Test is
How to perform the chair stand test correctly
How many times older adults may be expected to stand in 30 seconds
Why age and sex affect chair-stand scores
What a low chair-stand score may mean
How leg strength relates to mobility and independence
Why lower-body strength matters for everyday activities
How clinicians use functional tests when assessing older adults


Chapters

00:00 How Many Chair Stands Can You Do?
00:18 What Is the 30-Second Chair Stand Test?
00:49 How to Do the Chair Stand Test
01:24 What Does Your Score Mean?
01:42 Normal Scores by Age
02:04 What a Low Score Can Tell You
02:20 Leg Strength, Mobility & Independence
03:02 Next Test: 10-Second Balance Test


The standard CDC protocol uses a straight-backed chair without armrests with a seat approximately 17 inches (43 cm) high. Sit with your feet flat on the floor and arms crossed over your chest, then stand fully and sit back down as many times as possible in 30 seconds.

There is no single normal score for every older adult. CDC reference thresholds vary according to age and sex, and performance can also be affected by mobility limitations, pain, balance, medical conditions, and the testing setup.

The chair stand test is a screening and functional assessment, not a diagnosis of disease or biological age. If your score is lower than expected, it may be worth discussing your mobility, strength, exercise program, or fall risk with a healthcare professional.

If you feel dizzy, unstable, have significant pain, chest discomfort, or feel unsafe standing without your hands, do not perform the test alone.
